L10  /  Pathological basis of oral & systemic disease

Neurological Disorders

Why neurons are so easily and permanently injured, and the disorders a dentist meets: stroke, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, trigeminal neuralgia, peripheral neuropathy, Alzheimer and Parkinson disease.

Lecturer
Dr Joseph Ryan
Sections
15
Core reading
Underwood’s ch. 26
Key topics
Stroke · Epilepsy · TN
01

Organisation of the nervous system

Two anatomical divisions, two functional ones, and the differences that decide disease.

Anatomical

Central nervous system (CNS)

Brain + spinal cord. Integrates, processes and coordinates all sensory input and motor output. Protected by skull, vertebrae, meninges and CSF.

  • Grey matter — neuronal cell bodies, synapses
  • White matter — myelinated axons (myelin from oligodendrocytes)
Anatomical

Peripheral nervous system (PNS)

All nerves and ganglia outside the CNS — cranial nerves, spinal nerves, autonomic and sensory ganglia. Connects the CNS to limbs, organs and tissues.

Functional

Somatic nervous system

Voluntary motor control and conscious sensation (touch, pain, temperature, proprioception).

Functional

Autonomic nervous system (ANS)

Involuntary control of smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands. Sympathetic = “fight or flight”; parasympathetic = “rest and digest”; the enteric nervous system coordinates the gut.

The four structural distinctions that matter for pathology

 CNSPNS
Myelinating cellOligodendrocyte — myelinates multiple axonsSchwann cell — myelinates a single axon segment
Blood–brain barrierPresentAbsent in most regions
RegenerationPoorBetter — Schwann-cell–mediated repair
Typical diseaseMS (attacks oligodendrocyte myelin)Guillain–Barré (attacks Schwann-cell myelin)
Keep them apart

One Oligodendrocyte → Odles of axons (CNS). One Schwann cell → a Single segment (PNS). Because each oligodendrocyte serves many axons, losing one demyelinates several — a reason CNS demyelination (MS) produces such patchy, multi-tract deficits.

From the lecture slides
02

Brain regions and what they do

Localisation: the site of a lesion predicts the deficit.

LobeFunctionsDamage gives…
FrontalVoluntary movement (primary motor cortex), executive function, planning, judgement, personality and behaviourContralateral weakness; behavioural change
ParietalSomatic sensation (touch, pain, proprioception), spatial awareness and body orientationSensory loss; visuospatial problems
TemporalMemory formation, auditory processing, mood and language comprehensionMemory loss; receptive language problems
OccipitalVisual processing and interpretationVisual field deficits

The cerebral cortex is the outer grey matter of the hemispheres, built of six neuronal layers. Because function is localised, cortical damage produces localised neurological deficits — which is how a clinician localises a lesion from the presenting signs.

Below the cortex

White matter

Myelinated tracts

Fast cortical–subcortical communication. Particularly vulnerable to hypoxia and traumatic shearing (diffuse axonal injury).

Deep grey

Basal ganglia

Muscle tone, posture and movement initiation. Dysfunction → movement disorders (rigidity, tremor) — e.g. Parkinson disease.

Deep grey

Thalamus

The major sensory relay to the cortex; also consciousness and alertness.

Hindbrain

Cerebellum

Fine movement, balance and gait, timing and precision of movement.

Hindbrain

Brainstem

Major tracts; cranial nerve nuclei III–XII (head and neck); vital centres (respiration, vomiting). Compact, so small lesions can be life-threatening.

Cord

Spinal cord

Central grey, peripheral white. Anterior horn cells = lower motor neurones; damage gives LMN signs: weakness, atrophy, fasciculations.

Dental link

Cranial nerve nuclei III–XII sit in the brainstem — including the trigeminal (V), facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X) and hypoglossal (XII) nuclei. A brainstem stroke can therefore affect facial sensation, facial movement, swallowing and the tongue.

A patient has new weakness of the right arm and face after a stroke. Which lobe and which side is most likely affected?

The left frontal lobe (primary motor cortex). Voluntary movement is controlled by the frontal lobe, and motor pathways cross, so a lesion in the left hemisphere produces right-sided (contralateral) weakness. This is the principle of lesion localisation from presenting signs.

From the lecture slides
03

Neurons and glial cells

The working cell and the five cells that support it.

The neuron

PartStructure and job
Cell body (soma)Nucleus, Nissl substance (RER), mitochondria. Protein synthesis and metabolism; integrates incoming signals.
DendritesHighly branched receptive processes; carry graded potentials toward the soma.
AxonSingle long process for impulse transmission; ends in synaptic terminals.
Myelin sheathInsulation; oligodendrocytes (CNS) or Schwann cells (PNS). Speeds conduction by saltatory conduction (impulse jumps between nodes).
SynapseChemical synapses use neurotransmitters (ACh, glutamate, GABA). Electrical synapses are rare in the human CNS.

Glial cells

CNS

Astrocytes

Metabolic and structural support; maintain the blood–brain barrier; regulate ions and take up neurotransmitter; form glial scars after injury.

CNS

Oligodendrocytes

Myelinate multiple axons; metabolic support to axons. Vulnerable in multiple sclerosis.

CNS

Microglia

Resident immune cells (specialised macrophages). Phagocytic; activated in injury and infection; produce inflammatory mediators.

PNS

Schwann cells

Myelinate one axon segment each; support regeneration; targeted in Guillain–Barré syndrome.

PNS

Satellite cells

Surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia; structural and metabolic support.

FeatureCNSPNS
Inflammatory cellsMicroglia (resident macrophages)Macrophages from the circulation
ProtectionBBB, meninges and CSFNo BBB; less anatomical protection
Response to injuryGlial scar formation limits regrowthAxonal regrowth possible if Schwann cells intact
Typical disordersMS, stroke, Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’sGuillain–Barré, peripheral neuropathies
Which glial cell is primarily responsible for CNS myelination, and which disease targets it?

Oligodendrocytes (each myelinating multiple axons). They are the target in multiple sclerosis. Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons and are the target in Guillain–Barré syndrome. Astrocytes support and scar; microglia are the immune cells.

From the lecture slides
04

Why neurons are so vulnerable

Four properties that turn a short insult into permanent damage.

  1. Long-lived, non-dividing cells
    Neurons are terminally differentiated and cannot undergo mitosis, so they cannot be replaced. Injuries often become permanent.
  2. Highly metabolically active
    Extremely high oxygen and glucose demand, total dependence on continuous aerobic metabolism, and minimal energy reserves → rapid failure during ischaemia.
  3. Sensitive to hypoxia, ischaemia and toxins
    The lecture states that even brief oxygen deprivation (5–10 minutes) can cause irreversible injury. Also vulnerable to excitotoxicity (glutamate-mediated damage), toxins, heavy metals, alcohol, chemotherapy and viruses.
  4. Axonal transport is essential
    Cargo (neurotransmitters, organelles, structural proteins) moves along microtubules by kinesin (outwards) and dynein (back to the soma). Disruption → axonal degeneration (diabetes, toxins, trauma).
Link to L2 and L4

In L2 terms, neurons are permanent (non-dividing) cells. In L4 terms, lost permanent cells cannot regenerate, so the tissue heals by repair — in the CNS this is gliosis, the brain’s equivalent of a scar.

Which feature best explains why CNS neurons are highly susceptible to hypoxic injury?

Dependence on continuous aerobic metabolism. Neurons have minimal glycogen reserves and cannot make enough ATP anaerobically, so within minutes of losing oxygen they run out of energy. They also cannot divide to replace lost cells, so the damage is permanent.

05

Patterns of CNS injury

Five ways nervous tissue responds — and how to date an infarct.

PatternWhat happensTypical setting
Neuronal necrosisAcute, severe injury. “Red neurons”: eosinophilic cytoplasm, shrunken nuclei.Hypoxia, ischaemia, toxins; stroke, prolonged seizures
ApoptosisProgrammed, energy-dependent, cell-controlled death → no inflammationDevelopment, some neurodegenerative disease, mild injury
DemyelinationLoss of myelin with relative preservation of axons → conduction slowing or blockImmune (MS), metabolic, toxic
GliosisThe universal response of the CNS to injury: astrocytes proliferate and enlarge (reactive astrocytes) → glial scar that inhibits axonal regenerationAny injury
Wallerian degenerationAfter transection: axon distal to the injury degenerates; myelin breaks down; macrophages clear itTrauma; more effective regeneration in PNS than CNS
Timing of red neurons

The lecture says red neurons appear “within hours”. Robbins gives the more precise figure of about 12–24 hours after the insult before they are visible on H&E — so a patient who dies within an hour or two of a stroke may show no histological change.

Link to L2

The brain is the classic site of liquefactive necrosis (L2): it has little supporting stroma and is rich in lipid and enzymes, so dead tissue liquefies and is removed by macrophages, leaving a cavity.

What is the universal response of the CNS to injury, and why does it matter for recovery?

Gliosis — proliferation and enlargement of astrocytes (reactive astrocytes), forming a glial scar. It walls off the damaged area but physically and chemically inhibits axonal regrowth, which is one reason CNS injuries rarely recover fully.

06

Cerebrovascular disease (stroke)

Definition, causes and the chain from lost blood flow to dead tissue.

Definition

A focal neurologic disorder caused by destruction of brain substance as a result of intracerebral haemorrhage, thrombosis, embolism or vascular insufficiency. Also known as stroke, cerebral apoplexy, brain attack.

Generally older: 50–80 yearsLecture: 3rd most common cause of mortality in Australia
~85% of strokes

Ischaemic

Vascular occlusion: embolic (e.g. clot from the heart in AF, or from a carotid plaque), thrombotic (on atherosclerotic plaque), dissection, vasculitis.

~15% of strokes

Haemorrhagic

A weakened vessel bursts, flooding the area with blood; the cells die because they lose supply and are compressed. Major risk factor: hypertension.

The ~85/15 split is the standard textbook figure, added for context; it is not on the slides.

Pathogenesis

Indiscriminate interruption of normal perfusion to brain parenchyma. Oxygen is imperative for normal CNS function, so the lecture’s chain is:

O₂ depletion → energy failure → failure of electrolyte homeostasis → cytotoxic oedema → cell death

Deficits depend on the territory

Visual fieldMotorSensoryVerbalCognitiveEmotional
Describe the pathophysiology of ischaemic stroke.

An artery is occluded (thrombus, embolus, dissection or vasculitis), so perfusion to a region of brain stops. Neurons depend on continuous aerobic metabolism, so oxygen depletion causes energy (ATP) failure. Without ATP the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase fails, sodium and water enter the cells (cytotoxic oedema), and depolarised neurons release glutamate, causing excitotoxic Ca²⁺ influx that activates destructive enzymes. Cells in the core die (infarction, liquefactive necrosis); the surrounding penumbra is salvageable if flow is restored quickly. Over time the infarct shows red neurons, then macrophages, then gliosis and a cavity.

From the lecture slides
07

Stroke: recognition, chair-side management and oral care

Symptoms, what to do if it happens in the surgery, and the patient afterwards.

Infarction

Death of tissue resulting from a failure of blood supply.

Clinical manifestations

Onset

Gradual or abrupt

Headache may precede the neurological signs; sudden severe headache (especially with haemorrhage).

Signs

Focal and usually one-sided

Numbness or weakness of face, arm or leg, especially on one side; confusion; trouble speaking or understanding; difficulty walking, dizziness, loss of balance or coordination.

F.A.S.T.

Face drooping · Arm weakness · Speech difficulty · Time to call 000. (Public-health mnemonic used in Australia — a convenient way to remember the slide’s signs.)

If a stroke occurs in the dental chair

  1. Discontinue the dental procedure
    Activate the dental office emergency team.
  2. Activate the emergency medical service
    Call an ambulance — stroke treatment is time-critical.
  3. Monitor vital signs
    Pulse, blood pressure, breathing, conscious state.
  4. Manage signs and symptoms
    Including basic life support if needed.
  5. Position the patient semi-supine
    Lay the chair back semi-supine.
  6. Administer oxygen
    As per the lecture’s management slide.

Oral manifestations and considerations

Bleeding

Anticoagulant / antiplatelet therapy

Patients are generally on anticoagulants → plan for post-extraction bleeding.

Saliva

Xerostomia

A side effect of their medications → caries risk.

Function

Orofacial weakness

Poor control of oral secretions, reduced gag reflex, impaired mastication → poor nutrition and aspiration risk.

From the lecture slides
08

Multiple sclerosis

Autoimmune demyelination of the CNS — and why the face may show it first.

Definition

A relapsing, remitting, autoimmune, inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. The immune system attacks the myelin sheath, causing communication problems between the brain and the rest of the body.

Symptoms

Patchy and variable

Numbness, weakness (generally one side), electric-shock-like sensations, tremor, lack of coordination; neurological deficits can result.

Risk factors

Who gets it

Age 20–40; women > men; family history; low vitamin D; smoking.

“Relapsing-remitting” is the commonest course, not the only one

About 85% of patients start with relapsing-remitting MS; others have a progressive course from onset (primary progressive), and many relapsing patients later become secondary progressive. Pathologically the lesion is the plaque: a sharply defined area of demyelination with relative axonal preservation and gliosis, typically around ventricles and in the optic nerves, brainstem and spinal cord.

Oral manifestations and dental considerations

  • Paraesthesia or numbness of orofacial structures, or trigeminal neuralgia, may be one of the first signs of MS. (A young patient with trigeminal neuralgia should raise this possibility.)
  • Some patients need physical assistance because of muscle weakness.
  • Conscious sedation / GA are likely to exacerbate symptoms.
  • May be on corticosteroids → HPA suppression (adrenal crisis risk with stress).
  • MS can make good oral hygiene impossible.
  • Placement of FPD/RPD should be based not only on oral findings but on the patient’s physical ability to maintain oral health.
Link to L5B

MS is an organ-specific autoimmune disease driven mainly by autoreactive T cells against myelin antigens — the L5B ideas of loss of tolerance and genetic + environmental triggers apply directly.

Which is the hallmark pathological process in MS?

Autoimmune demyelination of CNS axons. Oligodendrocyte myelin is destroyed while axons are relatively preserved (at least early), so conduction slows or blocks. It is not Schwann-cell dysfunction (that is PNS) and not primarily neuronal apoptosis.

From the lecture slides
09

Epilepsy and seizure types

Seizure is the event; epilepsy is the tendency.

Definitions

Epilepsy: a chronic neurological disorder characterised by recurrent seizures.
Seizure: a sign of a disease, manifesting as an episodic disturbance of movement, feeling or consciousness, caused by sudden synchronous, inappropriate and excessive electrical discharges that interfere with normal brain function.

Most cases

Idiopathic (primary)

Generally a specific cause cannot be determined.

Cause known

Acquired (secondary)

Metabolic, structural or functional abnormalities — including head trauma, especially with loss of consciousness for more than 30 minutes.

Partial vs generalised

 Partial (focal)Generalised
WhereRestricted to discrete areas of cortexBoth hemispheres simultaneously, bilaterally symmetric
Usual causeStructural abnormalities of the brainCellular, biochemical or structural abnormalities with wider distribution
SubtypesSimple — consciousness fully preserved; motor, sensory or autonomic symptoms
Complex — consciousness impaired; cannot respond to commands
Secondary generalised		Tonic–clonic, absence, myoclonic, atonic, infantile
Petit mal

Absence seizures

Sudden brief lapses of consciousness without loss of postural control; last seconds; consciousness returns suddenly; can have many a day.

Grand mal

Generalised tonic–clonic

The type most commonly produced by metabolic derangements. Starts with tonic muscle contraction; after 10–20 s it evolves into the clonic phase (alternating relaxation and contraction). Usually lasts ~1 minute.

Terminology you will meet elsewhere

The lecture uses the older terms. The current ILAE (2017) classification renames simple partial as focal aware, complex partial as focal impaired awareness, and secondary generalised as focal to bilateral tonic–clonic. Same seizures, new names.

10

Epilepsy in the dental chair

Oral effects, the history to take, and what to do during a seizure.

Oral manifestations and considerations

Trigger

Stress and fatigue

Increase the probability of a seizure — keep appointments calm and short.

Drugs

Gingival hyperplasia

Several anticonvulsants, classically phenytoin, cause gingival overgrowth.

Trauma

Injuries

Seizures can cause traumatic injuries to the oral cavity (tongue biting, fractured teeth).

Wear

Faceting

Intense clenching gives wear facets when seizures are frequent and severe.

Prosthetics

Design for safety

Design prostheses to minimise the risk of damage or displacement (aspiration risk).

Questions to ask

Background

At the medical history

How long have you had epilepsy? What type of seizures? How often? Which medications? How do they begin — any warning? Can you respond during one? Confused or tired afterwards? When was the last one?

Day of appointment

Before you start

Taken your medication today, and correctly over the past few days? Any other drugs today (OTC, alcohol, illicit)? Tired or unusually stressed? Any recent illness or seizures?

Managing a seizure in the chair

  1. Terminate the dental procedure
    Remove instruments from the mouth if it can be done safely; do not force anything between the teeth.
  2. Position the patient comfortably
    Protect from injury; note the time.
  3. If the seizure stops
    Reassure the patient → allow them to recover → discharge (with an escort).
  4. If the seizure continues > 5 minutes
    Summon medical assistance and give basic life support as indicated. A seizure lasting over 5 minutes is treated as status epilepticus, a medical emergency.
Describe the clinical relevance of epilepsy for dental practice.

(1) Seizure risk during treatment — stress, fatigue and missed medication increase it, so take a seizure history, check medication compliance on the day, and have a plan (stop, protect, time it, call for help if > 5 min). (2) Drug effects — anticonvulsant-induced gingival hyperplasia. (3) Trauma — fractured teeth, lacerations, wear facets from clenching. (4) Prosthodontics — design appliances that resist fracture and displacement to avoid aspiration.

From the lecture slides
11

Trigeminal neuralgia

Paroxysmal electric-shock pain in CN V, its criteria, mechanism and treatment.

Definition

Sudden, usually unilateral, severe, brief stabbing pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve — described as one of the most painful conditions in medicine.

Incidence 4.3–27 / 100,000Females > males

ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria

ARecurrent paroxysms of unilateral facial pain in one or more trigeminal divisions, no radiation beyond, fulfilling B and C
BPain has all of: (1) lasting a fraction of a second to 2 minutes; (2) severe intensity; (3) electric shock-like, shooting, stabbing or sharp
CPrecipitated by innocuous stimuli within the affected distribution
DNot better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis

The slide labels two criteria “B”; the lettering above follows the published ICHD-3.

Classical vs secondary

The slide’s figures show the spectrum of vessel–nerve contact (proximity → contact → compression → distortion) and a mass in the basal cisterns. Classical TN = neurovascular compression. Secondary TN = an underlying disease such as a tumour (e.g. at the cerebellopontine angle) or MS (a demyelinating plaque in the pons). This is why MRI is part of the work-up.

Treatment

First line

Medications

Textbook first choice is carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine), which stabilises the hyperexcitable nerve membrane. The lecture lists “medications” without naming them.

Refractory

Surgical management

Radiofrequency trigeminal rhizotomy · Gamma knife radiosurgery · Glycerol rhizolysis · Microvascular decompression (moves the vessel off the nerve, with a Teflon pad — treats the cause).

Describe the neural mechanism underlying classical trigeminal neuralgia.

A vascular loop (most often the superior cerebellar artery) compresses the trigeminal nerve at its root entry zone. Chronic pulsatile compression causes focal demyelination. Bare axons lie against one another, allowing ephaptic transmission (cross-talk) and ectopic, high-frequency discharges, so input from large touch fibres spills into pain pathways. Light touch in a trigger zone therefore evokes a brief paroxysm of electric-shock pain.

Peripheral neuropathy

Causes, and diabetic neuropathy in detail.

CauseKey points
Diabetes mellitusMost common cause worldwide; metabolic + microvascular injury; sensory, motor and autonomic dysfunction
Chronic alcoholDirect neurotoxicity + thiamine (B1) deficiency; axonal degeneration
Vitamin deficiencyB1 → beriberi neuropathy; B6 → both deficiency and excess cause neuropathy; B12 → subacute combined degeneration, sensory ataxia
DrugsChemotherapy (vincristine, cisplatin), antiretrovirals, isoniazid (B6-dependent), amiodarone, metronidazole
ToxinsLead, arsenic, mercury; industrial solvents; organophosphates
OtherHypothyroidism, autoimmune neuropathies, paraneoplastic syndromes

Diabetic neuropathy

Commonest

Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy

“Glove and stocking” sensory loss; burning, tingling, numbness; loss of vibration and proprioception; painless injuries.

Autonomic

Autonomic neuropathy

Gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, bladder dysfunction, reduced sweating.

Motor

Motor neuropathy

Wasting of intrinsic foot muscles → altered gait, deformities.

Complication

Foot ulcers & Charcot joint

Sensory loss + autonomic change + poor healing → major cause of lower-limb amputation.

Oral and craniofacial relevance

Burning mouth syndrome · altered taste · xerostomia (autonomic involvement) · altered trigeminal sensation → risk during dental procedures (the patient may not feel trauma).

Link to L11+12

Diabetic neuropathy is one of the microvascular complications of diabetes (with retinopathy and nephropathy) covered in the endocrinopathies lecture.

13

Neurodegeneration: Alzheimer and Parkinson disease

Misfolded proteins, selective vulnerability, and two classic diseases.

Principles of neurodegeneration

  1. Protein misfolding and aggregation
    Misfolded proteins accumulate when proteasomal and lysosomal clearance fails; aggregates disrupt synapses and are toxic.
  2. Selective neuronal vulnerability
    Specific populations degenerate — hippocampus in Alzheimer’s, substantia nigra in Parkinson’s. The pattern of loss gives the clinical picture.
  3. Chronic, progressive course
    Slow, insidious onset over years; irreversible loss of neurons and synapses.
  4. Neuroinflammation
    Microglial activation contributes to damage and accelerates progression.
 Alzheimer diseaseParkinson disease
Key factMost common cause of dementia (up to 70%); usually > 65 yDegeneration of the substantia nigra pars compacta
Lost cellsCortical and hippocampal neuronsDopaminergic neurons → ↓ dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway
ProteinAβ plaques (extracellular, from amyloid precursor protein) + neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau (intracellular)Lewy bodies — intracytoplasmic inclusions of α-synuclein (hallmark; also in Lewy body dementia)
GrossCortical atrophy, marked hippocampal shrinkage, enlarged ventriclesPale substantia nigra (loss of pigmented neurons)
ClinicalEarly short-term memory loss → language, visuospatial → executive and behavioural change, loss of independenceResting “pill-rolling” tremor, rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel), bradykinesia, later postural instability
OtherRisk: age (strongest), APOE-ε4, family history, vascular risk factors, prior TBINon-motor: constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, cognitive change
Which lesion correlates with symptoms?

In Alzheimer disease it is the neurofibrillary tangles that correlate strongly with severity of cognitive decline. Pathology maps to symptoms: hippocampus → memory; parietal → visuospatial; frontal → behaviour.

Contrast the characteristic protein aggregates of Alzheimer and Parkinson disease.

Alzheimer: extracellular amyloid plaques (Aβ peptide cleaved from amyloid precursor protein) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau. Parkinson: intracytoplasmic Lewy bodies made of α-synuclein in surviving dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra. Both reflect failure to clear misfolded proteins.

From the lecture slides
14

Oral considerations in Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s

Same goal, different obstacles: movement in PD, cognition in AD.

PD

Parkinson disease

  • Motor impairment (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia) → difficulty with oral hygiene
  • Drooling (sialorrhoea) from impaired swallowing, not excess saliva
  • Seborrhoeic dermatitis around the mouth
  • Xerostomia from anticholinergic drugs
  • ↑ caries and periodontal risk (plaque)
  • Dysphagia and aspiration risk
  • Orofacial pain / burning mouth occasionally
AD

Alzheimer disease

  • Cognitive decline → reduced ability to maintain oral hygiene
  • Difficulty understanding instructions
  • Agitation, resistance to care
  • Xerostomia from cholinesterase inhibitors, antidepressants, antipsychotics
  • High risk of candidiasis and periodontal disease
  • Malnutrition if chewing/swallowing compromised
  • Forgetting dentures → loss, breakage, poor fit, aspiration
The sialorrhoea trap

Drooling in Parkinson disease is not from making too much saliva — it is from not swallowing it (reduced, slowed swallowing and flexed posture). The same patient may also have a dry mouth from anticholinergic medication.

Shared management

Short, simple appointmentsMorning scheduling — symptoms best controlledInvolve carers/family: consent, planning, post-op careHigh caries risk: fluoride, CPP-ACP, saliva substitutesModified aids: electric brushes, adapted handles, interdental brushesAvoid sedatives/anticholinergics where possibleMonitor swallowing; avoid aspiration-prone procedures
15

Summary, tutorial scenario and glossary

The lecture’s take-home points, worked through.

1

Structure predicts pathology

Neurons are long-lived, non-dividing and highly metabolically active → vulnerable to hypoxia, toxins, trauma. Glia decide the pattern of injury, repair and inflammation. CNS vs PNS myelin shapes demyelinating disease.

2

Disease categories

Vascular (stroke, haemorrhage, global ischaemia) · degenerative (Alzheimer, Parkinson, motor neuron disease) · peripheral neuropathies (diabetic, toxic, nutritional).

3

Diagnostic principles

Injury timing shows in morphology (red neurons → macrophages → gliosis/cavity). Focal vs diffuse processes give distinct pictures. Combined CNS + PNS involvement changes prognosis.

4

Dental relevance

Communication and memory; motor control (difficulty keeping the mouth open); airway, swallowing, aspiration; salivary flow, hygiene and caries. Adapt sedation, ergonomics and appointment planning.

Tutorial scenario

A patient reports electric-shock pain radiating from the lower lip three months after removal of tooth 37. The pain is triggered by light touch. What pain mechanism is likely, and what investigations and management are indicated?

Mechanism: neuropathic pain from injury to the inferior alveolar nerve during the extraction — ICHD-3 calls this painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy. The damaged nerve develops ectopic discharges and lowered thresholds, so light touch (allodynia) provokes shock-like pain. It mimics trigeminal neuralgia, but the clear temporal link to trauma, a defined nerve territory and usually accompanying numbness or altered sensation point to post-traumatic neuropathy.

Investigations: careful pain history; neurosensory testing of the lip and chin (light touch, two-point discrimination, pin-prick, thermal) and mapping of the affected area; radiograph (OPG/CBCT) to look at the socket and canal (root fragment, relationship to the canal); MRI if features suggest classical or secondary trigeminal neuralgia.

Management: explain and reassure; refer to oral medicine / orofacial pain; avoid further surgery at the site; neuropathic pain medication is specialist-directed (e.g. carbamazepine if TN-like, or agents such as pregabalin or amitriptyline); review and document sensory change over time.

Glossary

Oligodendrocyte
CNS glial cell that myelinates multiple axons; target in MS.
Schwann cell
PNS glial cell that myelinates one axon segment; supports regeneration; target in Guillain–Barré.
Astrocyte
CNS support cell; maintains the BBB; forms the glial scar.
Microglia
Resident immune (macrophage) cells of the CNS.
Saltatory conduction
Impulse “jumping” between nodes of a myelinated axon, increasing speed.
Red neuron
Acutely necrotic neuron: eosinophilic cytoplasm, shrunken nucleus.
Gliosis
Reactive astrocyte proliferation and enlargement; the CNS response to injury.
Wallerian degeneration
Degeneration of an axon distal to a point of transection.
Excitotoxicity
Neuronal injury from excess glutamate stimulation and Ca²⁺ influx.
Penumbra
Underperfused but salvageable tissue around an infarct core.
Infarction
Death of tissue resulting from failure of blood supply.
Seizure
Episodic disturbance from sudden synchronous, excessive neuronal discharge.
Status epilepticus
A seizure lasting over 5 minutes (or repeated without recovery): an emergency.
Ephaptic transmission
Abnormal electrical cross-talk between adjacent demyelinated axons.
Microvascular decompression
Surgery separating a vessel from the trigeminal root.
Lewy body
Intracytoplasmic α-synuclein inclusion; hallmark of Parkinson disease.
Neurofibrillary tangle
Intraneuronal aggregate of hyperphosphorylated tau.
Sialorrhoea
Drooling; in PD from impaired swallowing, not excess saliva.
